```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(scales)
library(reshape2)

# Folder that contains the two CSV files
data_dir <- "."
```

# 4.1 Load the data

```{r load}
pop <- as.data.frame(readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "world_population.csv"),
                                     show_col_types = FALSE))

# The "²" in two column names can break on some systems, so i gave them plain ASCII names
names(pop)[grepl("^Area", names(pop))]    <- "Area_km2"
names(pop)[grepl("^Density", names(pop))] <- "Density_km2"

co2 <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "CO2_emission.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)   # year columns become X1990 ... X2019
```

Two things to notice about the CO2 file:

* It contains the **2019 column twice** (`X2019` and `X2019.1`, identical values), so we drop the copy.
* The unit is **metric tons per capita**, not total tonnes.

```{r co2-clean}
#here we are checking if the two columns are identical,if they are we print true and we delete one by setting it to null
all.equal(co2$X2019, co2$X2019.1)
co2$X2019.1 <- NULL
```

# 4.2 Exploratory data analysis (World Population Dataset)

```{r eda-basic}
names(pop)                 # variable names
head(pop, 5)               # top 5 rows
tail(pop, 10)              # bottom 10 rows
str(pop)                   # data types
dim(pop)                   # shape (rows, columns)
```

## Duplicates and missing values

```{r eda-dups}
cat("Duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(pop)), "\n")
pop <- pop[!duplicated(pop), ]          # drop duplicates

colSums(is.na(pop))                     # missing values per column
```

## Outliers (box plots)

```{r eda-outliers, fig.height=6}
quant_vars <- c("2022 Population", "Area_km2", "Density_km2",
                "Growth Rate", "World Population Percentage")

long <- pop |>
  select(all_of(quant_vars)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

p_box <- ggplot(long, aes(y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", outlier.colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Box plots of quantitative variables", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("boxplots.png", plot = p_box, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
p_box   # show the graph in the report

# How many outliers by the 1.5 x IQR rule?
iqr_outliers <- sapply(quant_vars, function(v) {
  x <- pop[[v]]; q <- quantile(x, c(.25, .75)); i <- diff(q)
  sum(x < q[1] - 1.5 * i | x > q[2] + 1.5 * i)
})
iqr_outliers
```

### Handling missing values and outliers

* **Missing values:** none were found.

```{r outlier-handling}
num_cols <- names(pop)[sapply(pop, is.numeric)]
for (v in num_cols) pop[[v]][is.na(pop[[v]])] <- median(pop[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)

pop <- pop |>
  mutate(log_pop2022   = log10(`2022 Population`),
         log_area      = log10(Area_km2),
         log_density   = log10(Density_km2))
```

# 4.3 New variable: projected 2030 population

The model is $N_t = P e^{rt}$ with $P$ = 2022 population and $t = 2030 - 2022 = 8$ years.

```{r projection}
t_years <- 2030 - 2022
pop <- pop |>
  mutate(r = log(`Growth Rate`),
         pop_2030 = `2022 Population` * exp(r * t_years))

pop |>
  select(`Country/Territory`, `2022 Population`, `Growth Rate`, pop_2030) |>
  arrange(desc(pop_2030)) |>
  mutate(pop_2030 = round(pop_2030)) |>
  head(10)
```

# 4.4 Top ten most populous countries

```{r top10}
top10 <- pop |> arrange(desc(`2022 Population`)) |> slice_head(n = 10)
top10$`Country/Territory`
```

## 1. Population in 2022


```{r top10-bar}
p_top10_bar <- ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(`Country/Territory`, `2022 Population`),
                  y = `2022 Population`)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`2022 Population` / 1e6, 1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = "Ten most populous countries, 2022",
       x = NULL, y = "Population (millions)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("top10_population_2022.png", plot = p_top10_bar, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_top10_bar   # show the graph in the report
```

## 2. Population trend 1990–2022

The dataset only contains census-year snapshots (1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2022), not every year,
so the trend is drawn through those points.

```{r top10-trend}
trend <- top10 |>
  select(country = `Country/Territory`, `1990 Population`, `2000 Population`,
         `2010 Population`, `2015 Population`, `2020 Population`, `2022 Population`) |>
  pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "year", values_to = "population") |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(substr(year, 1, 4)))

p_trend <- ggplot(trend, aes(year, population, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(trend$year)) +
  labs(title = "Population trend of the 10 most populous countries, 1990-2022",
       subtitle = "Log scale so that smaller countries remain readable",
       x = "Year", y = "Population (millions, log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("population_trend_1990_2022.png", plot = p_trend, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_trend   # show the graph in the report
```

## 3. CO2 emission trend 1990–2019

The CO2 file uses World Bank country names, so a few names differ from the population file
(for example *Russian Federation* vs *Russia*). We harmonise them first.

```{r name-map}
name_map <- c("Bahamas, The" = "Bahamas", "Brunei Darussalam" = "Brunei",
  "Cabo Verde" = "Cape Verde", "Congo, Dem. Rep." = "DR Congo",
  "Congo, Rep." = "Republic of the Congo", "Cote d'Ivoire" = "Ivory Coast",
  "Egypt, Arab Rep." = "Egypt", "Gambia, The" = "Gambia",
  "Hong Kong SAR, China" = "Hong Kong", "Iran, Islamic Rep." = "Iran",
  "Korea, Dem. People's Rep." = "North Korea", "Korea, Rep." = "South Korea",
  "Kyrgyz Republic" = "Kyrgyzstan", "Lao PDR" = "Laos",
  "Macao SAR, China" = "Macau", "Micronesia, Fed. Sts." = "Micronesia",
  "Russian Federation" = "Russia", "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)" = "Sint Maarten",
  "Slovak Republic" = "Slovakia", "St. Kitts and Nevis" = "Saint Kitts and Nevis",
  "St. Lucia" = "Saint Lucia", "St. Martin (French part)" = "Saint Martin",
  "St. Vincent and the Grenadines" = "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines",
  "Syrian Arab Republic" = "Syria", "Turkiye" = "Turkey",
  "Venezuela, RB" = "Venezuela", "Virgin Islands (U.S.)" = "United States Virgin Islands",
  "West Bank and Gaza" = "Palestine", "Yemen, Rep." = "Yemen")

co2$Country <- ifelse(co2$Country.Name %in% names(name_map),
                      name_map[co2$Country.Name], co2$Country.Name)

# Names that still do not match (these are simply absent from one of the files)
setdiff(co2$Country, pop$`Country/Territory`)
```

```{r co2-trend}
co2_top <- co2 |>
  filter(Country %in% top10$`Country/Territory`) |>
  select(Country, starts_with("X")) |>
  pivot_longer(-Country, names_to = "year", values_to = "co2") |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(sub("X", "", year)))

p_co2_trend <- ggplot(co2_top, aes(year, co2, colour = Country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "CO2 emissions of the 10 most populous countries, 1990-2019",
       x = "Year", y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("co2_trend_1990_2019.png", plot = p_co2_trend, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_co2_trend   # show the graph in the report
```

# 4.5 Correlation analysis

## 1. Area, Density, Growth Rate and World Population Percentage

```{r corr}
vars <- pop |>
  select(Area = Area_km2, Density = Density_km2,
         Growth_Rate = `Growth Rate`, World_Pop_Pct = `World Population Percentage`)

cor_p <- round(cor(vars, method = "pearson"), 2)
cor_s <- round(cor(vars, method = "spearman"), 2)
cor_p   # Pearson (sensitive to outliers)
cor_s   # Spearman (rank based, robust to outliers)
```

```{r corr-heatmap}
heat <- function(m, ttl) {
  ggplot(melt(m), aes(Var1, Var2, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = value), size = 4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
    labs(title = ttl, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
    theme_minimal()
}
p_heat_pearson  <- heat(cor_p, "Pearson correlation heatmap")
p_heat_spearman <- heat(cor_s, "Spearman correlation heatmap")

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("heatmap_pearson.png", plot = p_heat_pearson, width = 6, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_heat_pearson   # show the graph in the report

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("heatmap_spearman.png", plot = p_heat_spearman, width = 6, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_heat_spearman   # show the graph in the report
```

## 2. Population (2022) versus CO2 emissions (2019)

```{r merge}
merged <- pop |>
  select(Country = `Country/Territory`, Continent, CCA3,
         pop2022 = `2022 Population`) |>
  inner_join(co2 |> select(Country, Region, co2_2019 = X2019), by = "Country") |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_2019))

dim(merged)
head(merged)
```

```{r pop-co2-plot}
p_pop_co2 <- ggplot(merged, aes(pop2022, co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Continent), alpha = .8, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", se = TRUE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(title = "Population (2022) vs per-capita CO2 emissions (2019)",
       x = "Population, millions (log scale)",
       y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("population_vs_co2.png", plot = p_pop_co2, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_pop_co2   # show the graph in the report
```

```{r pop-co2-stats}
cor.test(merged$pop2022, merged$co2_2019, method = "pearson")
cor.test(merged$pop2022, merged$co2_2019, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

fit <- lm(co2_2019 ~ log10(pop2022), data = merged)
summary(fit)
```

**Interpretation.** Because the CO2 variable is *per capita*, a large population does not
automatically mean higher per-capita emissions. The correlation is expected to be weak:
per-capita emissions are driven mainly by income, energy mix and industrial structure, not by
country size. Spearman and the log-scale regression are preferred over raw Pearson because
population is extremely right-skewed.

# 4.6 CO2 emissions by continent (2019)

The 2019 values are summed by continent (continent comes from the population dataset).

```{r continent}
cont <- merged |>
  group_by(Continent) |>
  summarise(total_co2 = sum(co2_2019), n_countries = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(total_co2))
cont

p_continent <- ggplot(cont, aes(reorder(Continent, -total_co2), total_co2, fill = Continent)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(total_co2, 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(title = "Sum of 2019 CO2 emissions by continent",
       x = NULL, y = "Sum of CO2 (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Save this graph as a PNG in the working directory
ggsave("co2_by_continent_2019.png", plot = p_continent, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_continent   # show the graph in the report
```

```{r answers, results='asis'}
cat("1. **Highest emitting continent:** ", cont$Continent[1],
    " (", round(cont$total_co2[1], 2), ")\n\n", sep = "")
cat("2. **Third continent:** ", cont$Continent[3],
    " — total ", round(cont$total_co2[3], 2), " metric tons per capita\n\n", sep = "")
cat("3. **Last continent:** ", cont$Continent[nrow(cont)],
    " — total ", round(cont$total_co2[nrow(cont)], 2), " metric tons per capita\n", sep = "")
```

```{r continent-mean}
merged |>
  group_by(Continent) |>
  summarise(mean_co2 = round(mean(co2_2019), 2), n_countries = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_co2))
```
